## sns-no-target

**Level:** error · **amtool:** also catches it

**What goes wrong:** An `sns_configs` entry has no destination. None of `topic_arn`,
`phone_number` or `target_arn` is set.

```yaml title="Bad"
receivers:
  - name: team
    sns_configs:
      - sigv4:
          region: us-east-2
        # no topic_arn, phone_number or target_arn
```

**What Alertmanager does:** Rejects the config.

**How to fix:** Set one of `topic_arn` (an SNS topic), `phone_number` (SMS) or
`target_arn` (a mobile push endpoint).

```yaml title="Fixed"
receivers:
  - name: team
    sns_configs:
      - topic_arn: 'arn:aws:sns:us-east-2:123456789012:My-Topic'
        sigv4:
          region: us-east-2
```


---

Source: https://danikdanik2013.github.io/amlint/checks/inhibition/

# Inhibition checks

These checks catch inhibition rules that mute more alerts than you meant, or that mute each
other so nobody gets notified.

An **inhibition rule** (an entry under `inhibit_rules:`) mutes alerts that match its
*target* matchers while an alert that matches its *source* matchers is firing, but only
when both alerts have the same values for the labels listed in `equal:`. **Matchers** are
label conditions such as `severity="critical"`. amlint reads both styles:
`source_matchers` / `target_matchers`, and the older `source_match` / `source_match_re` /
`target_match` / `target_match_re`.

To see whether one alert mutes another, run
[`amlint route alertmanager.yml alertname=DiskFull --firing 'alertname=NodeDown'`](../usage.md#inhibition).

---

## inhibit-no-equal

**Level:** warn · **amtool:** doesn't catch it

**What goes wrong:** An inhibition rule has no `equal:` field, so source and target alerts
don't need to have anything in common.

```yaml title="Bad"
inhibit_rules:
  - source_matchers: [severity="critical"]
    target_matchers: [severity="warning"]
    # no equal:
```

**What Alertmanager does:** Loads the config. While any critical alert fires, it mutes every
warning alert, in every cluster and service. A critical alert in one service hides warnings
from unrelated ones.

**How to fix:** List the labels that tie a target alert to its source, such as the alert
name and the cluster.

```yaml title="Fixed"
inhibit_rules:
  - source_matchers: [severity="critical"]
    target_matchers: [severity="warning"]
    equal: [alertname, cluster]   # only mute warnings of the same alert on the same cluster
```

**Limits:** Rules with no source matchers at all are not flagged. Every alert counts as
their source, so they mute their targets whenever any alert that isn't a target fires. That
is a deliberate "always mute" pattern: kube-prometheus uses it to keep its `InfoInhibitor`
alert quiet.

---

## circular-inhibition

**Level:** warn · **amtool:** doesn't catch it

**What goes wrong:** Two inhibition rules can mute each other: the source of each rule
matches the target of the other.

```yaml title="Bad"
inhibit_rules:
  - source_matchers: [severity="critical"]
    target_matchers: [severity="warning"]
    equal: [alertname]
  - source_matchers: [severity="warning"]    # the first rule's target...
    target_matchers: [severity="critical"]   # ...mutes the first rule's source
    equal: [alertname]
```

**What Alertmanager does:** Loads the config. When a critical and a warning alert with the
same `alertname` fire together, each mutes the other, and you get no notification for
either. A muted alert still mutes others.

**How to fix:** Keep only the direction you need, usually the more severe alert muting the
less severe one.

```yaml title="Fixed"
inhibit_rules:
  - source_matchers: [severity="critical"]
    target_matchers: [severity="warning"]
    equal: [alertname]
```

**Limits:** amlint compares only the `label="value"` matchers of each side. Regex and `!=`
matchers are ignored, so a pair of rules that differ only in those can still be flagged.

---

## inhibit-same-match

**Level:** info · **amtool:** doesn't catch it

**What goes wrong:** The source and target side of an inhibition rule require the same
`label="value"`, such as `severity="critical"` on both sides. The rule then mutes alerts of
the same kind as the alerts that trigger it.

```yaml title="Bad"
inhibit_rules:
  - source_matchers: [severity="critical", env="prod"]
    target_matchers: [severity="critical", team="infra"]   # same severity as the source
    equal: [alertname]
```

**What Alertmanager does:** Loads the config. A critical `env="prod"` alert mutes critical
`team="infra"` alerts with the same `alertname`, including ones that are sources of this
rule themselves. An alert never mutes itself, and two alerts that both match both sides
don't mute each other. If both sides match exactly the same alerts, the rule mutes nothing.

**How to fix:** If a critical alert should only mute less severe ones, change the target
side. If critical alerts are meant to mute other critical alerts, keep the rule and turn
the finding off with `# amlint: disable=inhibit-same-match` at the end of the rule's first
line.

```yaml title="Fixed"
inhibit_rules:
  - source_matchers: [severity="critical", env="prod"]
    target_matchers: [severity="warning", team="infra"]
    equal: [alertname]
```

**Limits:** Like [`circular-inhibition`](#circular-inhibition), this compares only
`label="value"` matchers.


---

Source: https://danikdanik2013.github.io/amlint/checks/timing/

# Timing checks

These checks catch notification timing that doesn't do what it says, and routes that point
at time intervals that don't exist.

Alertmanager batches alerts into **groups** (alerts on the same route that share its
`group_by` labels) and times each group's notifications with three settings:

- **`group_wait`**: how long to wait after a group's first alert before the first
  notification. Default `30s`.
- **`group_interval`**: how often to notify about changes, such as new or resolved alerts,
  to a group that was already notified. Default `5m`.
- **`repeat_interval`**: how long to wait before sending a notification again for alerts
  that are still firing and unchanged. Default `4h`.

A child route inherits any of these it doesn't set from its parent, and the root route
falls back to the defaults. amlint works out the values the same way, and reports a finding
on the route that sets one of the two values involved.

---

## repeat-before-group

**Level:** warn · **amtool:** doesn't catch it

**What goes wrong:** `repeat_interval` is shorter than `group_interval`.

```yaml title="Bad"
route:
  receiver: default
  group_interval: 1h
  repeat_interval: 15m   # shorter than group_interval
```

**What Alertmanager does:** Loads the config. After the first notification, Alertmanager
sends a group's notifications only once per `group_interval`, and re-sends still-firing
alerts at the first of those sends after `repeat_interval` has passed. So the reminders
come every hour, not every 15 minutes.

**How to fix:** Make `repeat_interval` at least as long as `group_interval`, ideally a
multiple of it. To get reminders more often, shorten `group_interval` too.

```yaml title="Fixed"
route:
  receiver: default
  group_interval: 5m
  repeat_interval: 15m   # a multiple of group_interval
```

---

## wait-exceeds-interval

**Level:** warn · **amtool:** doesn't catch it

**What goes wrong:** `group_wait` is longer than `group_interval`. The two values are
usually swapped: `group_wait` is meant to be a short pause that collects the first burst of
alerts.

```yaml title="Bad"
route:
  receiver: default
  group_wait: 10m       # wait 10 minutes before the first notification
  group_interval: 2m    # but report changes every 2 minutes
```

**What Alertmanager does:** Loads the config. A new group waits the full 10 minutes before
its first notification; after that, changes go out every 2 minutes. The first notification
about a new problem is the slowest one.

**How to fix:** Keep `group_wait` shorter than `group_interval`.

```yaml title="Fixed"
route:
  receiver: default
  group_wait: 30s
  group_interval: 5m
```

---

## undefined-time-interval

**Level:** error · **amtool:** also catches it

**What goes wrong:** A route's `mute_time_intervals` (mute the route during these times) or
`active_time_intervals` (send only during these times) names an interval that isn't
defined under `time_intervals:`.

```yaml title="Bad"
route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - matchers: [team="infra"]
      receiver: infra
      mute_time_intervals: [maintenance]   # not defined anywhere
```

**What Alertmanager does:** Refuses to load the config:
`undefined time interval "maintenance" used in route`.

**How to fix:** Define the interval under `time_intervals:`, or fix the name. Intervals
defined under the older top-level `mute_time_intervals:` key count too.

```yaml title="Fixed"
route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - matchers: [team="infra"]
      receiver: infra
      mute_time_intervals: [maintenance]
time_intervals:
  - name: maintenance
    time_intervals:
      - weekdays: [saturday, sunday]
```

---

## global-resolve-timeout-missing

**Level:** info · **amtool:** doesn't catch it

**What goes wrong:** `global.resolve_timeout` isn't set, so Alertmanager uses its default
of `5m`. Nothing breaks; the value just isn't visible in your config.

```yaml title="Bad"
route:
  receiver: default
# no global.resolve_timeout
```

**What Alertmanager does:** Uses `resolve_timeout` only for alerts that arrive without an
end time (`endsAt`): if such an alert isn't sent again within that time, Alertmanager marks
it resolved. Prometheus always sets an end time, so this setting doesn't change alerts that
come from Prometheus.

**How to fix:** Set the value you want. If all your alerts come from Prometheus, you can
ignore this check instead (see [Ignoring checks](index.md#ignoring-checks)).

```yaml title="Fixed"
global:
  resolve_timeout: 5m
route:
  receiver: default
```


---

Source: https://danikdanik2013.github.io/amlint/checks/rules/

# Prometheus rules checks

These checks compare your Alertmanager config with your Prometheus **alerting rules**, the
`alert:` rules in Prometheus rule files that fire alerts named after the rule. They catch
parts of `alertmanager.yml` that wait for an alert no rule fires (usually a typo or a
renamed rule), and alerts that fall through to your catch-all destination because nothing
more specific picks them up. They run only when you pass your rule files with `--rules`:

```bash
amlint check alertmanager.yml --rules 'rules/*.yml'
```

## Which rule files amlint reads

- Quote the glob so that amlint expands it, not your shell. `**` matches subdirectories:
  `--rules 'rules/**/*.yml'`.
- Repeat `--rules` for more locations:
  `--rules 'rules/*.yml' --rules 'k8s/prometheusrules/*.yaml'`.
- amlint reads Prometheus rule files (`groups[].rules[]`), the format that Prometheus,
  Thanos, Mimir and the Loki ruler use. It also reads prometheus-operator `PrometheusRule`
  manifests (`spec.groups`): several in one file separated by `---`, or a `kind: List` as
  `kubectl get prometheusrules -o yaml` prints it.
- Only alerting rules (`alert:`) count. amlint skips recording rules (`record:`).
- If a glob matches no file, or a file can't be parsed, amlint exits with code 2. If the
  files contain no alerting rules, amlint prints a warning and skips these checks.

## What amlint knows about an alert

Alertmanager routes an alert by its labels: each route, a branch of the `route:` tree,
sends the alerts its matchers select to a receiver, a named notification destination. At
runtime an alert gets its labels from four places:

1. the series that the rule's PromQL `expr` returns (`instance`, `job`, `namespace`, ...)
2. the rule's `labels:`
3. `alertname`, which is always the rule's name
4. Prometheus' `external_labels`, the labels a Prometheus server adds to every alert it
   sends (set in `prometheus.yml`, often `cluster` or `region`)

Only 2 and 3 are in the rule file. Together they are the rule's **static labels**, and
amlint checks routing with those. This matters because routes often match on labels that
only exist at runtime, such as `namespace` or `cluster`, and amlint can only be sure about
the labels it can see. So:

- A label whose value is a Go template (`team: '{{ $labels.owner }}'`) has an unknown
  value.
- A label that routes match on but that no rule sets (`namespace`, `cluster`, `job`) is
  assumed to come from the series or `external_labels`, so its value is unknown too.
- A label that some rules set but this rule doesn't is treated as absent, the way
  Alertmanager would see it. That's how amlint catches a rule that forgot its `severity`
  label.

When a result depends on a label with an unknown value, amlint reports nothing rather than
guess. amlint also can't see `alert_relabel_configs` in Prometheus, which can change labels
on the way out.

All three checks are warn or info, never error. `amtool check-config`, Alertmanager's own
config checker, catches none of them, because the config itself is valid. Each finding
points at a line in `alertmanager.yml`, so `# amlint: disable=<code>` comments work there
as usual.

---

## route-unknown-alertname

**Level:** warn · **amtool:** doesn't catch it

**What goes wrong:** A route matches an `alertname` that no alerting rule in your
`--rules` files fires. Usually the name has a typo, or the rule was renamed or removed.

```yaml title="rules/node.yml"
groups:
  - name: node
    rules:
      - alert: HighCPUUsage
        expr: node_cpu_busy > 0.9
```

```yaml title="alertmanager.yml (bad)"
route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - matchers: [alertname="HighCpuUsage"]   # no rule fires this name
      receiver: infra-pager
```

```
  ⚠  WARN   [route-unknown-alertname]  ·  alertmanager.yml:4:7  ·  route.routes[0]
     Route matches alertname 'HighCpuUsage', which no alerting rule in the --rules files
     produces — did you mean 'HighCPUUsage'? Unless such alerts come from another source,
     this branch is dead.
```

**What Alertmanager does:** Loads the config and runs. The route never receives the alert
it was written for, so the alert goes to whichever route matches it instead, often the
default receiver.

**How to fix:** Use the exact rule name. The finding suggests the closest one.

```yaml title="alertmanager.yml (fixed)"
route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - matchers: [alertname="HighCPUUsage"]
      receiver: infra-pager
```

**What amlint checks** in `matchers:`, `match:` and `match_re:`:

- `alertname="X"` (or `match: {alertname: X}`): `X` must be a rule's name.
- A regex that just lists names, such as `alertname=~"A|B|C"` (or `^(?:A|B|C)$`): amlint
  checks each name on its own, so it reports one misspelled entry in a long list.
- Any other regex, such as `alertname=~"Kube.*"`: amlint reports it when it matches none of
  the alert names. Like Alertmanager, it anchors the regex at both ends and uses Go RE2
  syntax.
- `!=` and `!~`: excluding a name that nothing fires excludes nothing, so that's probably a
  typo too.

**Limits:** Alerts that don't come from these rule files (another Prometheus, Loki,
Grafana, a script posting to the Alertmanager API) also look unknown. Pass their rule files
too, or add `# amlint: disable=route-unknown-alertname` to that route.

---

## inhibit-unknown-alertname

**Level:** warn · **amtool:** doesn't catch it

**What goes wrong:** An inhibit rule (a rule that mutes alerts matching its target while an
alert matching its source is firing) has a source or target that matches an `alertname` no
alerting rule fires. amlint checks `source_match`, `source_match_re` and `source_matchers`,
and the same `target_*` keys, with the same matching as
[`route-unknown-alertname`](#route-unknown-alertname).

```yaml title="rules/node.yml"
groups:
  - name: node
    rules:
      - alert: NodeDown
        expr: up{job="node"} == 0
      - alert: NodeHighLoad
        expr: node_load5 > 10
```

```yaml title="alertmanager.yml (bad)"
inhibit_rules:
  - source_matchers: [alertname="NodeDwn"]   # typo: no rule fires this
    target_matchers: [alertname="NodeHighLoad"]
    equal: [instance]
```

**What Alertmanager does:** Loads the rule and gives no sign of a problem. If the source
never fires, the rule never mutes anything. If the target never fires, the rule has
nothing to mute.

**How to fix:** Use the exact rule names.

```yaml title="alertmanager.yml (fixed)"
inhibit_rules:
  - source_matchers: [alertname="NodeDown"]
    target_matchers: [alertname="NodeHighLoad"]
    equal: [instance]
```

**Limits:** The same as for [`route-unknown-alertname`](#route-unknown-alertname). Alerts
from other sources look unknown.

---

## alert-hits-default-receiver

**Level:** info · **amtool:** doesn't catch it

**What goes wrong:** Based on its static labels, an alert matches none of the child routes
(the `routes:` under the top-level `route:`), so it goes to the default receiver, the
`receiver:` set at the top of `route:`. Typically the rule forgot its `severity` or `team`
label, or uses a value that no route handles.

```yaml title="rules/app.yml"
groups:
  - name: app
    rules:
      - alert: DiskFull
        expr: disk_free_ratio < 0.05
        labels:
          severity: critical
      - alert: QueueBacklog
        expr: queue_depth > 1000   # no severity label
```

```yaml title="alertmanager.yml"
route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - matchers: [severity="critical"]
      receiver: pager
```

```
  ℹ  INFO   [alert-hits-default-receiver]  ·  alertmanager.yml:1:1  ·  route
     Based on static rule labels, 1 alert with no severity label matches no child route and
     goes to the root receiver 'default': QueueBacklog (rules/app.yml:8). Labels from the
     PromQL series or external_labels may still route it elsewhere at runtime.
```

**What Alertmanager does:** Delivers these alerts to the default receiver, which is often
a channel nobody watches.

**How to fix:** Add the missing label to the rule, or add a route for the alert.

```yaml title="rules/app.yml (fixed)"
groups:
  - name: app
    rules:
      - alert: DiskFull
        expr: disk_free_ratio < 0.05
        labels:
          severity: critical
      - alert: QueueBacklog
        expr: queue_depth > 1000
        labels:
          severity: critical
```

If some alerts should use the default receiver, give them a route of their own
(`alertname=~"A|B"` to `default`). That also documents the choice. Or turn the check off
for the file with `# amlint: disable-file=alert-hits-default-receiver`.

**How findings are grouped:** amlint routes each rule with the same simulation as
[`amlint route`](../usage.md#route). You get one finding per combination of the label
values that the routes match on, and each finding names the first five alerts. So if you
send every warning to the default receiver on purpose, as kube-prometheus does, you get one
finding for `severity=warning`, however many warning alerts there are. A rule that lacks a
label the other rules set gets a finding of its own ("with no severity label"). All of
these findings point at the root `route:`.

**Limits:**

- It's info, not warn, because static labels aren't the whole story. amlint treats a label
  that this rule doesn't set as absent. If the label actually comes from the PromQL series
  or `external_labels`, the alert may still route elsewhere at runtime.
- amlint skips an alert when its route depends on a label with an unknown value (see
  [above](#what-amlint-knows-about-an-alert)).
- If the root route has no child routes, everything goes to its receiver by design, and
  the check stays quiet.


---

Source: https://danikdanik2013.github.io/amlint/contributing/

# Contributing

This page gets you from a fresh clone to a pull request: set up, run the tests CI runs, and
add a check. The last two sections cover the tests against the real Alertmanager and the
browser playground, which you only need when you work on those parts.

## Set up { #setup }

```bash
git clone https://github.com/danikdanik2013/amlint
cd amlint
pip install -e ".[dev]"
```

You need Python 3.9 or later. This installs amlint in editable mode, so `amlint` runs your
working copy, plus pytest, ruff and Hypothesis.

## Run the tests { #running-tests }

CI runs these on Python 3.9 to 3.15:

```bash
ruff check amlint/
pytest test_linter.py test_formats.py test_lsp.py -v
```

- `test_linter.py` covers the checks and the CLI.
- `test_formats.py` covers the input formats on the [Kubernetes & Mimir](kubernetes.md) page.
- Add `--cov=amlint` for coverage.

## Add a check { #how-to-add-a-new-check }

Every check is a function in
[`amlint/linter.py`](https://github.com/danikdanik2013/amlint/blob/main/amlint/linter.py).
It takes the parsed config as a dict and returns a list of findings.

**1. Write the function.**

```python
def check_your_rule(cfg: dict) -> List[Finding]:
    out: List[Finding] = []
    route = _root_route(cfg)
    if not route:
        return out
    for node, path in _walk_routes(route):
        if something_is_wrong(node):
            out.append(Finding(
                WARN,              # ERROR, WARN or INFO
                "your-rule-code",  # unique kebab-case code
                "What's wrong, and what happens to alerts because of it.",
                path,              # where in the config, e.g. route.routes[0]
            ))
    return out
```

`_walk_routes` yields every route with its path. The CLI turns the path into
`file:line:col`, in every input format.

**2. Register it** in `ALL_CHECKS` in the same file:

```python
ALL_CHECKS = [
    ...
    check_your_rule,
]
```

**3. Explain it.** Add an entry for `your-rule-code` to `EXPLAINS` in
[`amlint/explains.py`](https://github.com/danikdanik2013/amlint/blob/main/amlint/explains.py),
with `level`, `summary`, `why`, `bad` and `good`. `amlint list` and `amlint explain` read it,
and `--ignore` warns about codes that aren't there. Also add the code to `_DOCS_PAGES` in
the same file, under the docs page you document it on (step 5): editors link each finding
to that section.

If Alertmanager refuses to load a config that your check flags, also add the code to
`ALSO_CAUGHT_BY_AMTOOL` in the same file. The
[differential tests](#differential-tests-against-alertmanager) then check that
`amtool check-config` agrees.

**4. Add a test** to `test_linter.py`:

```python
def test_your_rule():
    cfg = {
        "route": {"receiver": "a"},
        "receivers": [{"name": "a"}],
        # the smallest config that triggers the rule
    }
    assert "your-rule-code" in codes(cfg)
```

**5. Document it.** Add a `## your-rule-code` section to the right page under `docs/checks/`,
and a row to the table in `docs/checks/index.md`. The playground links each finding to its
section by that heading.

## Pick a severity { #severity-guide }

| Level | Use when |
|-------|----------|
| `ERROR` | Alertmanager refuses to load the config, or alerts will be lost |
| `WARN` | Almost certainly not what the author meant |
| `INFO` | Suspicious and worth a look, but may be on purpose |

## Open a pull request { #opening-a-pr }

- One check or one fix per pull request is easiest to review.
- Include a test that fails without your change and passes with it.
- `ruff check amlint/` and `pytest test_linter.py test_formats.py test_lsp.py` pass.
- For a new check, add its docs (step 5 above).
- Add a line to `CHANGELOG.md` under `## [Unreleased]`.
- If you changed the docs, `mkdocs build --strict` passes (`pip install mkdocs-material`).

## Differential tests against Alertmanager

amlint simulates Alertmanager's routing, inhibition and config errors in Python. These tests
compare it with the real Alertmanager on generated configs. The
[fidelity page](fidelity.md) explains what that guarantees users. Run them with one command:

```bash
scripts/differential.sh
```

The script downloads an Alertmanager release (0.34.1 by default) into
`.cache/alertmanager/` and checks the tarball's sha256 against the release's
`sha256sums.txt`. Then it runs `tests/differential/` with that release's `amtool` and
`alertmanager` first on `PATH`. Extra arguments go to pytest.

| Test | Compares |
|---|---|
| `test_routing.py` | amlint's receivers with `amtool config routes test`, on generated configs and label sets |
| `test_validation.py` | `amtool check-config` rejects a config exactly when amlint reports an error whose code is in `ALSO_CAUGHT_BY_AMTOOL` |
| `test_inhibition.py` | alerts POSTed to a running `alertmanager`: each one's `status.inhibitedBy` and receivers with amlint's simulation |

Settings, as environment variables:

| Variable | Default | What it sets |
|---|---|---|
| `AM_VERSION` | `0.34.1` | the Alertmanager release |
| `AM_SHA256` | none | the tarball's sha256, checked as well (CI pins it) |
| `AMLINT_DIFF_SEED` | `0` | the Hypothesis seed: the same seed generates the same cases |
| `AMLINT_DIFF_EXAMPLES` | `300` | generated configs per routing and validation test |
| `AMLINT_DIFF_INHIBIT_EXAMPLES` | `40` | inhibition scenarios, each on its own `alertmanager` |

```bash
AM_VERSION=0.32.2 scripts/differential.sh                                  # another release
AMLINT_DIFF_SEED=7 AMLINT_DIFF_EXAMPLES=2000 scripts/differential.sh -x   # explore more
```

- The pytest header prints the seed and the number of examples, so you can replay a CI run
  with the same values.
- On a mismatch, the test reduces the case to a minimal config and label set. It prints both
  results and the `amtool` command that reproduces it.
- Plain `pytest` skips these tests when `amtool` isn't on `PATH`.

**In CI**, `.github/workflows/differential.yml` runs them against the last two minor
Alertmanager releases and the newest, on pull requests and pushes to `main` that touch
`amlint/routing.py`, `linter.py`, `goyaml.py`, `formats.py`, `explains.py` or the
differential tests. It also runs weekly with a fresh seed and more examples, and you can
start it by hand with a seed of your choice. When the weekly run warns that a newer
Alertmanager is out, add it to the workflow's matrix with its sha256, and update the
versions on the fidelity page and in the README.

**When a test fails**, the mismatch is one of two things:

- a bug in amlint: fix it, and add a regression test to `test_linter.py`
- a deliberate difference or an Alertmanager bug: document it under
  [Known differences](fidelity.md#known-differences), and teach the test to recognize it,
  narrowly

## The playground

[The playground](playground/index.md) runs amlint in the browser with
[Pyodide](https://pyodide.org) (Python compiled to WebAssembly).

| File | What it does |
|---|---|
| `docs/playground/app.js` | the UI |
| `docs/playground/worker.js` | loads Pyodide and amlint in a Web Worker, off the main thread |
| `docs/playground/amlint_playground.py` | calls `amlint.cli.main([... "--format", "json"])` for check, route and diff, and builds the route tree |
| `overrides/playground.html` | the page template |
| `playground/build.py` | builds the amlint wheel, the CodeMirror editor bundle and the examples into `docs/playground/dist/` (not committed) |

New checks show up in the playground without any change there. A change to the JSON output
of `check`, `route` or `diff` may need one.

To work on the page locally (needs npm):

```bash
pip install mkdocs-material
python playground/build.py   # again after changing amlint/ or playground/
mkdocs serve                 # http://127.0.0.1:8000/amlint/playground/
```

`python playground/build.py --no-editor` skips rebuilding the editor bundle, if you already
have one.

The docs workflow runs a headless smoke test of the built site on pull requests. To run it
yourself:

```bash
mkdocs build --strict
python -m http.server 8000 --directory site &
cd playground && npx playwright install chromium && node smoke-test.mjs http://127.0.0.1:8000/playground/
```

The examples in the playground's menu are listed in `EXAMPLES` in `playground/build.py`.
Their files are in `playground/examples/` and `testdata/`.
